strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a clear gap in surveillance video understanding: multimodal queries with temporal grounding are underexplored despite being practically important

Solid benchmark contribution (ForeSeaQA): First to jointly evaluate accuracy and temporal localization under both text-only and multimodal query conditions with 1,041 carefully curated questions across 6 diverse subtasks

Comprehensive experimental validation with diverse baselines (5 Video LMMs, 2 RAG methods), thorough ablation studies (Table 2) demonstrating design choices, and generalization to open-domain benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench)
Well-designed semi-automated data engine with human verification and informative dataset statistics demonstrating non-trivial temporal positions and varied video lengths

Clear practical insights: person-centric retrieval as strong inductive bias for surveillance, multimodal embedding space avoiding information loss, and efficiency gains with 2.6s latency vs. 5.2-7.6s for retrieval baselines
Excellent presentation with clear figures (especially Fig. 1, 6), thorough supplementary material including prompt templates, and reproducible metric definitions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: ForeSea combines existing off-the-shelf components (ByteTrack, VISTA, VideoLLaMA3) without introducing novel methods or learned components. Primary contribution is system integration rather than scientific advancement.

Persistent temporal localization weakness undermines core claims: despite 11% improvement over VideoRAG, ForeSea achieves only 13.6% IoU compared to 66% accuracy, with the gap remaining consistent across ablations (8-12%). This suggests the problem remains far from solved, and baseline IoU values are concerningly low across all methods.

Dataset limitations: Single-source (UCF-Crime only), modest scale (1,041 questions), crime-focused domain bias, and critically missing inter-annotator agreement statistics for the manual verification stage, raising concerns about benchmark reliability

Insufficient error analysis: Limited investigation of failure modes beyond qualitative examples; 'counting task is hardest' is noted but not analyzed. Missing systematic study of which person types, activities, or temporal reasoning patterns are challenging.

Confounded generalization experiments: VideoMME/MLVU use frame-level indexing while ForeSeaQA uses person-centric indexing, making it unclear whether improvements derive from retrieval benefits or the specific indexing strategy. Human tracking quality assumed perfect with no failure mode analysis.

Incomplete ablation analysis: Limited justification for K=3; VISTA vs. alternatives minimally explored (only CLIP comparison in Appendix); unclear which components (person-centric bias, multimodal embeddings, or VideoLLaMA3) drive improvements

Missing practical considerations: No discussion of temporal localization metric appropriateness for forensic workflows (e.g., are ±5 second offsets acceptable?), no societal impact discussion despite privacy/bias concerns inherent to surveillance systems, and reproducibility hampered by lack of stated dataset release commitment

Evaluation metric concerns: Temporal IoU thresholds appear strict for forensic search where approximate answers may suffice; threshold choices (0, 0.1, 0.3) lack justification. Binary search conventions (Appendix C.3) seem ad-hoc.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: multimodal queries with temporal grounding in surveillance are underexplored and practically relevant
ForeSeaQA benchmark contribution: first benchmark for multimodal image+text queries with precise temporal annotations across six diverse subtasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple Video LMMs/RAG baselines, both query modalities, detailed ablations, efficiency analysis, and generalization studies on open-domain benchmarks
Efficient and practical system: achieves lower latency (2.6s) than retrieval-augmented baselines (5.2-7.6s) while maintaining higher accuracy
Justified design choices: unified multimodal embedding space empirically shown superior to text-only projection; ablations clearly demonstrate contribution of each component
Clear presentation: well-structured paper with informative figures and comprehensive supplementary materials including prompt templates and detailed metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ForeSea is primarily an engineering pipeline of existing components (ByteTrack + VISTA + VideoLLaMA3) without novel algorithms or technical innovations. This reads as a systems/applications paper rather than research contribution suitable for ECCV

Small and domain-specific benchmark: 1,041 questions is modest compared to contemporary benchmarks; exclusively from UCF-Crime (crime/abnormal events) limits generalizability beyond forensic security domain

Weak data quality assurance: benchmark relies on LLM-based generation (Qwen) with unknown biases; manual verification process under-specified—no inter-annotator agreement scores, quality metrics, or detailed validation criteria reported

Core metric remains fundamentally weak: temporal IoU of 13.6% is low in absolute terms; claimed 11.0% improvement over VideoRAG misleads (2.8%→13.6% is low baseline improvement); paper acknowledges temporal grounding remains open problem. ForeSea-Global's 16.1% comes at cost of Search accuracy (57.5% vs 60.5%)

Benchmark potentially tailored to proposed method: person-centric queries emphasized in design; system uses person tracking; dataset favors this architectural choice rather than being neutral. Raises concerns about evaluation validity as general benchmark

Critical missing discussions: (1) No ethics/privacy discussion for surveillance system despite forensic search application; (2) No failure mode analysis (tracking failures, occlusions, multiple similar people); (3) Limited error categorization (only ~4 qualitative examples); (4) Insufficient ablation (only K∈{3,5} tested)

Reproducibility concerns: uses frontier/proprietary models (Qwen3-32B) for data generation; semi-automated pipeline difficult to reproduce; no code/data release plan mentioned; specific model versions and hyperparameters incompletely specified

Incomplete baseline comparisons and fairness issues: T* baseline achieves only 41.1%—concerning weakness; VideoLLaMA3 tested on full video processing (not its intended use); missing comparisons with other multimodal retrieval systems; VideoRAG may not be designed for this specific setting

Overstated generalization claims: on open-domain benchmarks, system switches to frame-level indexing (top-60+30 uniform) differing substantially from person-centric approach; modest gains on VideoMME (66.2% vs 65.6% VideoLLaMA3) and LongVideoBench (63.5%) don't strongly support generalization; not SOTA on these benchmarks

Unclear generalization of person-centric approach: all evaluation emphasizes person search; method inapplicable to videos without people or requiring global scene understanding; limited discussion of when this constraint is problematic

strengths: Novel benchmark (ForeSeaQA) addresses an important gap: multimodal queries with temporal grounding for forensic surveillance, which is practical and underexplored
High-quality benchmark design with thoughtful 4-stage semi-automated data engine, manual verification, joint answer+temporal evaluation, and diverse 6-subtask coverage (1,041 questions)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple strong baselines (5 VideoLLMs, 2 RAG systems), detailed ablations, task-specific analysis, and generalization to open-domain benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU)
Practical system design with clear advantages: person-centric retrieval as effective inductive bias, 2.6s latency (vs. 5.2-7.6s for baselines), 66.0% accuracy and 13.6% temporal IoU
Multimodal embedding approach (VISTA/GCL) properly avoids information loss compared to unimodal projection methods like CLIP
Well-written paper with excellent presentation, effective figures, and extensive supplementary material including data generation prompts and metrics definitions
Rigorous evaluation methodology with proper metrics, qualitative examples, and honest acknowledgment of limitations
weaknesses: System novelty is limited: ForeSea combines existing components (ByteTrack, GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3) with straightforward orchestration; the key insight that person-centric retrieval helps is valuable but relatively simple

Temporal localization performance remains weak: 13.6% IoU for ForeSea, with all methods in 8-16% range, suggesting the benchmark exposes a fundamental unsolved challenge rather than driving algorithmic progress

Multimodal query component underperforms expectations: multimodal accuracy (65.4%) is actually lower than text-only (66.7%), indicating the system does not effectively leverage image information; image encoding is simplistic (concatenation)

Benchmark limitations: 1,041 questions is modest; limited to UCF-Crime distribution (crime/anomaly focused) without diversity analysis; inter-annotator agreement not reported; scalability limited by manual verification bottleneck

Person-centric retrieval introduces trade-offs not adequately explored: accuracy-vs-IoU trade-off with ForeSea-Global variants, unknown robustness to tracking failures, poor fit for global events and anomalies

Generalization claims are overstated: on VideoMME, ForeSea (65.6%) underperforms VideoLLaMA3 (66.2%); on MLVU, ForeSea (73.0%) merely matches VideoLLaMA3; advantages primarily over prior RAG methods, not recent VideoLLMs

Limited failure analysis: no systematic categorization of error types, no investigation of performance variation with video length/complexity, insufficient justification for why K=5 retrieval hurts temporal precision
Data and code availability not explicitly stated, hindering reproducibility and community adoption
Missing discussion of ethical implications and responsible use of surveillance systems
Counting task identified as particularly difficult but no solutions or deeper analysis proposed

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap by introducing the first benchmark for multimodal, temporally-grounded video QA in surveillance domain with 1,041 carefully curated questions across six subtasks
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 VideoLMMs and multiple retrieval baselines with thorough ablation studies demonstrating key design choices
Clear diagnostic insights showing temporal localization as primary bottleneck (7-16% IoU for VideoLLMs) and multimodal query robustness as a key differentiator
Practical system design with demonstrated latency improvements (2.6s vs 5.2-7.6s) and strong generalization to open-domain benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench)
Well-supported benchmark construction with semi-automated generation, manual verification, and detailed evaluation metrics; comprehensive supplementary materials enhance reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in ForeSea system—combines mostly off-the-shelf components (ByteTrack, GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3) without significant algorithmic innovation

Critical evaluation gaps: no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported for manual QA verification despite 50% of LLM-generated questions being removed; single-domain benchmark source (UCF-Crime) with skewed scene distribution (69% indoor) limits generalization

Temporal grounding challenge remains severely unresolved with ForeSea achieving only 13.6% IoU; lack of systematic failure analysis for temporal tasks and no investigation of accuracy-IoU disconnect (85% accuracy but 15% IoU for Event tasks)

Evaluation methodology concerns: multiple-choice format doesn't reflect real-world forensic workflows; distractor selection process unclear; no systematic task difficulty analysis; averaging IoU across tasks masks high variance (Search 17.6% vs Temporal 8.2%)

Insufficient analysis of multimodal queries: no investigation of why they hurt performance or behavior when query images poorly match database content; retrieval quality varies substantially across encoders but domain-specific methods not explored

Missing societal impact discussion despite surveillance application raising privacy and fairness concerns; limited baseline comparisons (no person ReID or anomaly detection systems); no failure categorization beyond two qualitative examples

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: multimodal queries with temporal grounding for forensic surveillance is underexplored and practically relevant
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple Video LMMs, retrieval approaches, and ablation studies demonstrating rigorous methodology
ForeSeaQA benchmark is the first to jointly evaluate accuracy and temporal localization under multimodal query conditions
System achieves strong relative performance on multimodal queries where other models degrade significantly (65.4% vs 67.7% baseline drop of 6 points)
Generalization experiments on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench show framework applicability beyond surveillance
Well-motivated problem formulation with practical relevance for video forensics and surveillance analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ForeSea is a straightforward pipeline combining existing components (ByteTrack, GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3) without novel architectural or algorithmic contributions
Benchmark quality concerns: No inter-annotator agreement metrics reported; without κ values, impossible to assess annotation consistency or task validity

Critical red flag in temporal grounding: Oracle caption baseline achieves 83.2% MC accuracy but only 31.1% temporal IoU (52-point gap), suggesting temporal annotations may be poorly defined or fundamentally misaligned with video content

Across all methods, temporal IoU remains critically low (7-16%), indicating potential issues with benchmark formulation rather than just method limitations; paper acknowledges this but provides no investigation
Missing human baseline makes it impossible to assess benchmark difficulty or whether performance levels are acceptable

Benchmark size is modest (1,041 questions) compared to recent standards (e.g., SurveillanceVQA-589K); sourced exclusively from UCF-Crime dataset limiting domain diversity despite generalization claims

Weak generalization to open-domain benchmarks: On VideoMME and MLVU, ForeSea matches or slightly exceeds VideoLLaMA3 baseline but doesn't substantially improve over it; adaptation requires switching from person-centric to frame-level retrieval, undermining main contribution claim
No inter-annotator agreement or validation methodology for temporal boundary annotations (Ts, Te); precision and consistency unknown
Design choice justification lacking: K=3 appears arbitrary; person-centric assumption contradicted by superior performance of ForeSea-Global and ForeSea-Hybrid variants
Statistical rigor issues: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or cross-validation; per-subtask sample sizes are small given 1,041 total questions across 6 tasks
Incomplete failure analysis: No investigation of tracking failure modes, temporal grounding error patterns, or when person-centric retrieval is inappropriate (e.g., global anomaly/counting tasks)
Ethical and privacy concerns with forensic surveillance video analysis not discussed
Unclear if ForeSeaQA benchmark will be publicly released, limiting impact as a benchmark contribution
Data generation pipeline relies on proprietary LLM versions (Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B) affecting reproducibility; distractor selection methodology not detailed

strengths: Novel benchmark (ForeSeaQA) for multimodal video QA with precise temporal grounding in surveillance—first of its kind addressing realistic forensic workflows with image+text queries
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse state-of-the-art models (5 VideoLLMs, 2 RAG baselines) with extensive ablations on spatial grounding, encoder choices, and VLM backbones
Practical system (ForeSea) achieving strong results: 66.0% accuracy on ForeSeaQA, 65.4% on multimodal queries, outperforming 72B models with only 7B parameters
Insightful technical findings: person-centric retrieval as effective inductive bias, text-based coordinate injection outperforming visual modifications, multimodal queries exposing VideoLLM gaps
Careful dataset construction with semi-automated generation and rigorous human verification; datasets reflects realistic low-resolution surveillance with diverse scenes
Strong generalization demonstrated on open-domain benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench) with competitive or superior performance using only half the frames
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: detailed prompts, evaluation metrics in supplementary material, comprehensive implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ForeSea straightforwardly combines existing components (ByteTrack, GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3) with no novel architectures or training procedures

Concerning temporal localization gap: ForeSea achieves only 13.6% IoU despite 66% accuracy, indicating models answer without precise grounding; oracle caption baseline shows 83.2% accuracy but only 31.1% IoU, suggesting fundamental task difficulty not addressed

Data generation quality concerns: semi-automated LLM pipeline may introduce systematic biases; 50% rejection rate raises coverage vs. quality tradeoff; missing inter-annotator agreement metrics and bias analysis

Benchmark scope limitations: 1,041 questions is modest; single-source dataset (UCF-Crime); surveillance-specific; person-centric retrieval may not generalize as general principle (modest improvements on VideoMME)

Insufficient failure analysis: limited qualitative examples (6 cases), no systematic exploration of why certain tasks (e.g., temporal reasoning at 53-57%, counting) significantly underperform; paper acknowledges 'open challenges' without investigation

Critical missing information: uncertain whether ForeSeaQA will be publicly released, impacting reproducibility and community impact; no discussion of societal/ethical implications for surveillance and forensic analysis

Technical details underexplored: uniform sampling may lose temporal information without comparison; concatenating K=3 clips' effect on tokens unclear; limited correlation analysis between retrieval quality and end-to-end performance; no statistical significance testing
